tip: Greek orders with take: θα πάρω το ψάρι (tha páro to psári = I'll take the fish) – παίρνω (pérno) is the standard way to say I'll have at a restaurant.
After a preposition, me is μένα, not με: για μένα (ya ména = for me). The short με (me) only works attached to a verb.
Θα ήθελα (tha íthela = I would like) – θα plus a past form makes a request polite.
Χύμα (khíma = loose, unbottled): κρασί χύμα (krasí khíma) is house wine from the barrel, ordered by the carafe, not the bottle.
Τα γεμιστά (ta yemistá) – rice-stuffed tomatoes and peppers; the dish name is normally used in the plural.
Χορτοφάγος (khortofághos = vegetarian) is literally grass-eater.
You can answer yes by just repeating the verb: έχει αρκετό (ékhi arketó = it has plenty) – no ναι (ne = yes) needed.
Συστήνετε (sistínete = you recommend) is from συστήνω (sistíno), which also means to introduce someone.
The accent on μάς shows it means to us, not our: μάς σύστησε (mas sístise = he recommended to us).
Greek salad is the village salad: χωριάτικη (khoriátiki = village-style) – the word σαλάτα (saláta) is usually left out.
Πάει (pái = it goes) does the pricing work: πάει με το κιλό (pái me to kiló) is literally it goes with the kilo, meaning priced by the kilo.
First agrees like an adjective: έρχονται πρώτοι (érkhonde próti = they arrive first) – masculine plural to match μεζέδες (mezédes), not one fixed form.
Φτάνει (ftáni) also means it's enough: δεν φτάνει (den ftáni = it's not enough).
Greek keeps both negatives: κανείς δεν βιάζεται (kanís den viázete = nobody hurries, lit. nobody doesn't hurry).
The ending -άκι (-áki) makes a thing small and friendly: πιατάκια (piatákia = little plates), from πιάτο (piáto = plate).
Ποτέ (poté) normally means never, but in a best-or-worst comparison it means ever: που έφαγα ποτέ (pu éfagha poté = that I ever ate).
Θέλει (théli = wants) also does duty for needs: το ψάρι θέλει λεμόνι (to psári théli lemóni = fish needs lemon).
Το δικό μου (to dikó mu = mine) is the strong form; a plain μου (mu) after a noun just means my.
Δεν το μετανιώνω (den to metanióno = I don't regret it) – the little το stands for the whole decision, not one thing.
Και (ke) can mean also, not just and: ήρθε και ένα γλυκό (írthe ke éna ghlikó = a dessert came too) – before a noun it adds too or even.
Putting εγώ after the verb adds emphasis: πληρώνω εγώ (pliróno eghó = I'm the one paying). Handy, since Greeks often compete for the bill.
Treating someone has its own verb: κερνάω (kernáo) – απόψε κερνάω εγώ (apópse kernáo eghó = tonight I'm treating).
Χωρίζουμε τον λογαριασμό (khorízume ton loghariasmó = shall we split the bill) is understood, but the custom leans to one person treating the group.
Το φιλοδώρημα (to filodhórima = the tip) is not required in Greece – rounding up or leaving coins is the usual move.
Τα ψιλά (ta psilá = the small change) is literally the thin ones.
Βγαίνω (vyéno = come out) also does totals: βγήκε σαράντα (vyíke saránda = it came to forty).
Στην υγειά μας (stin iyá mas = to our health) is the standard toast – the everyday greeting γεια (ya) is the same word for health, shortened.
Greek coffee is ordered by sugar: σκέτο, μέτριο, γλυκό (skéto, métrio, ghlikó = plain, medium, sweet).
Spoken Greek often repeats the object with a short pronoun: τον καφέ τον πίνουμε (ton kafé ton pínume = the coffee, we drink it).
Στου Μήτσου (stu Mítsu = at Mitsos's place) – στου plus a name normally means at that person's place.
